methods.s_power: What a record this long can detect
methods.data_plain: Temperature and rain come from MERRA-2, a NASA model that blends many observations. For rain we also show GPM IMERG, a record from satellites and rain gauges, as a sensitivity check: the two share some inputs, so IMERG is not an independent confirmation. Every result says which kind of data it uses.
methods.data_experts: Region values are area-weighted means on each product's own grid (MERRA-2 0.5° × 0.625°; IMERG 0.1°), using the share of each cell inside the region. A region enters our set only when enough effective data cells cover it and only a small part of what its mean describes lies outside it. When two places are compared, a cell both touch goes to the one holding more of it, and each side must still keep enough cells. The screening map uses a conservative regrid to 1°. Input files are pinned by SHA-256 in the input manifest.
methods.seasons_plain: Months repeat every year: summers are hot and monsoons are wet. To see a long-term change we compare like with like: one value per year, or one per season (for example every June–September).
methods.seasons_experts: Temperatures use a day-weighted mean of the months; rain adds daily rate × days. A season and every rain total need all their months; a yearly temperature needs at least 10 of 12 months. Seasons that cross the new year are dated by the year in which they end. Space first, then time. Missing years stay missing; nothing is filled in.
methods.howmuch_plain: We draw the most typical slope through the years and say how much it changes per decade, with a 95% range: ranges made this way catch the true rate about 95 times in 100. It is not a 95% chance that this one range is right.
methods.howmuch_experts: Sen's slope (the median of all pairwise slopes, on actual years) with Conover's intercept. The range uses Sen's rank method with the Mann–Kendall variance inflated for memory and the multiplier 2.25 instead of 1.96: in our simulations 1.96 caught the true rate too rarely. The table shows how often each multiplier caught the true rate.
methods.significant_plain: A trend is “supported” when a pattern this clear would rarely appear from random ups and downs alone, after allowing for “memory” (a warm year is often followed by another warm year) and for the number of tests we ran.
methods.significant_experts: MK-AR1: Mann–Kendall with a tie-corrected variance, inflated by 1 + 2Σ(1 − k/n)φ̃ᵏ, where φ̂ is the AR(1) coefficient of a regression of each year on the year before, with an intercept and a trend (consecutive years only), bias-corrected as φ̃ = (nφ̂ + 2)/(n − 4) and clipped to [0, 0.95]. p uses the normal approximation with a continuity correction. A least-squares t-test with effective sample size is shown for comparison and never decides.
methods.domain_plain: We tested the method on many kinds of made-up records. It works well on some and badly on others, so we give verdicts only on the kinds where it works. Elsewhere we show the slope and say “no verdict: outside the range this method was tested for”. The table gives the largest year-to-year memory allowed for each record length.
methods.domain_experts: A verdict needs temperature or rain; the whole year or a pre-registered season; at least 20 complete years (15–19 are exploratory); no missing year; memory φ̃ at or below φ_max(n), the largest memory at which the calibrated false-alarm rate stays at or below 8%; and a pooled leftover-memory check across the region's data cells that finds no memory beyond what AR(1) describes. Stress tests: when the true trend is zero, records whose memory mixes a fast and a slow part, and AR(2) records, make any such test too eager; our domain checks lower those rates, and the table shows by how much.
methods.family_plain: Before we looked at any trend in real data, we wrote down and committed exactly which places, pairs, seasons and thresholds we would test. Only those tests get verdict words. Everything else is exploration.
methods.family_experts: The confirmatory family (for each pre-registered pair and each variable: both regions' yearly trends and the trend in their difference) uses Holm's correction; the secondary family of season tests uses Benjamini–Hochberg.
methods.compare_plain: “A trend here, none there” does not show that two places changed differently. We subtract one place from the other, year by year, and test the trend in that difference. Each place's own rate is shown beside it, never subtracted.
methods.compare_experts: The estimand is the trend in d(t) = A(t) − B(t), with its own Sen slope, range and MK-AR1 test; it is not Sen(A) − Sen(B). Labels: “opposite fitted directions” (descriptive only), “supported opposite trends” (both regions supported, opposite signs), “rates differ” (the difference is supported). Tested on made-up pairs with known answers:
methods.checks_plain: Before we accept a trend, we try to break it: a missing year, other start and end years, a change in the data rather than in the Earth.
methods.checks_experts: Coverage and gaps; documented data changes, each reviewed by a person for headline cases; leave-one-year-out; five other windows (robustness checks, not new claims). A doubt lowers the grade. The Pettitt test flags a sudden jump and never changes a verdict.
methods.grade_plain: Strong evidence: adjusted p below α/5 and no doubts. Supported trend: adjusted p below α and at most one doubt. Can't tell yet, which is not the same as no change: everything else. Whether the change is big enough to matter is answered separately, against a threshold declared in advance.
methods.power_plain: A short or noisy record can miss a real change. The table shows how often the test catches a trend of a given size (in standard deviations of the yearly noise, per year) in records of each length.
methods.power_experts: Power of MK-AR1 by simulation with an injected trend. The verdict card shows no “years needed” number.
methods.maps_plain: If you test thousands of places, some will look like trends by chance. We control the share of false alarms among the cells that stand out (false discovery rate 10%) and hatch the places we cannot test. The map is for exploring and gives no verdicts.
methods.maps_experts: Per 1° cell, MK-AR1 with memory pooled over the 5 × 5 neighbourhood and the leftover-memory check; Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.10 over the testable cells within each map.
methods.map_null_none: This build has no pure-noise map test.
methods.tests_plain: Golden tests assert values, tolerances and verdicts, and any mismatch fails the build.
methods.breaks_plain: Known changes in how each record was made. A person reviews each one that falls inside a headline case's years; the outcome is shown on that result.
methods.limits_plain: No forecasts. No claims about causes: at most, a result is “consistent with” a process. Linear trends only; jumps are flagged. Places smaller than the data cells are not in our set. Variables other than temperature and rain are not analysed in this release.
methods.reproduce_plain: Every result file is public and carries its build id, the input-manifest hash and the pre-registration hash. The same pinned inputs, pre-registration and code give the same files.

methods.golden: This build: {passed} of {total} golden tests passed.

watch.lead: Each case plays step by step on the real screens, with a caption for every step. Pause at any time, or take over and investigate yourself.
watch.ending_supported: The evidence supports the claim, with the checks and the numbers shown. Open the case to look at it yourself.
watch.ending_cant_tell: We can't tell yet. That is not the same as no change: the record is too short or too noisy to decide.
watch.ending_none: Open the case to look at each result yourself.
watch.family_size: One of {n} tests we registered in advance.

offline.how_to_get: The offline version is one HTML file with these cases inside. It opens by double-click, with no internet.

data.lead: The NASA records behind every result, how to cite them, and the other material the site uses.
data.boundaries: Region boundaries: geoBoundaries and Natural Earth, with the licence recorded for each file.
data.outlines: Map outlines: Natural Earth 1:110m (public domain), simplified and bundled with the site. The globe wears NASA's Blue Marble image (public domain), also bundled.
data.power: NASA POWER (cross-check only): these data were obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project funded through the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program.
data.no_logos: The site uses NASA data. It shows no NASA logo and is not endorsed by NASA.

ai.lead: How we used AI tools to build this project, and where we did not use them.
ai.how_1: Planning: we asked many AI advisors (several models, each given a role such as statistician or skeptic) to critique our plan, had two research tools fact-check the claims, merged the advice by fixed rules, let our own simulation code settle every statistical dispute, and had a different model red-team the merged plan.
ai.how_2: Specification and engine: an AI assistant helped write our specification (documents, data formats, test cases with expected values) and wrote the statistics engine from it. The engine's numbers were checked against an earlier set of expected values, by simulation studies whose rules were fixed before they ran, and by tests that rebuild every example exactly.
ai.how_3: Code: AI coding assistants wrote the data pipeline and this website from that specification, checked by tests and read by a person.
ai.how_4: Language: AI drafted Bangla and English interface text, which a native Bangla reader checks.
ai.how_5: People decided the design, the statistical methods, every threshold, the regions and the comparisons, and we committed those choices before we looked at any real trend.
ai.product_body: No AI computes, changes or words any number. Every value, verdict and sentence on screen comes from one tested Python engine and fixed templates.
ai.media_body: No AI-generated images, video or audio are used on this site.
ai.record_body: The repository keeps an AI-use statement and a log of every coding-agent session (docs/AI_USE.md and docs/ai_log/).

about.body_1: CaseFile Earth is a NASA Space Apps 2026 project for the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!”. It treats every trend as a case: it lines up the data that could answer a question, tests the trend, and shows a graded verdict or “can't tell yet”, with the evidence attached.
about.body_2: It covers Bangladesh, its divisions and nearby regions, in English and Bangla, and a 1° screening map of the whole planet for exploring. The site works offline from a single file.
about.role_a_body: Holds the methods, the pre-registration and the results build.
about.role_b_body: Builds the data pipeline from NASA archives and publishes the site.
about.role_c_body: Builds the screens, the watch cases and the words in both languages.
about.licence_data: NASA data: NASA open data; cite each record as listed on the Data & credits page.
about.licence_fonts: Fonts: Instrument Serif, Inter Tight, Noto Serif Bengali, Noto Sans Bengali and IBM Plex Mono (SIL Open Font License), bundled with the site.
about.licence_outlines: Map outlines: Natural Earth (public domain) through world-atlas (ISC). Earth image: NASA Blue Marble (public domain).
about.licence_libs: Libraries: React, globe.gl and three.js, Observable Plot, d3-scale-chromatic, Radix, Tailwind CSS, Motion and Zustand, each under its own open-source licence.
about.challenge_body: The challenge asks for a tool that helps people select Earth data, see how it changed, and say what changed, where, by how much and whether the change stands out from chance. CaseFile Earth answers it for temperature and rain, and tests the difference between two places directly.
